w: Behind the west towers sits the Great East Window, the largest expanse of medieval stained glass on Earth, glazed with a full Last Judgment. The first church here dates to 627; the current Gothic pile mostly to 1220-1472. The north transept's Five Sisters window climbs sixteen metres in grey-green grisaille glass.
s: The largest medieval stained-glass window on Earth
_facts: First record of a church on the site dates to 627
Bulk of the building was constructed between 1220 and 1472
East window depicts the Last Judgment and is the largest expanse of medieval stained glass in the world
Five Sisters window has five lancets each over 53 feet (16.3m) high, filled with grisaille glass

w: Its quatrefoil keep looks almost jaunty from the riverbank, but Clifford's Tower marks one of England's darkest nights: in 1190, around 150 local Jews took refuge inside during a mob siege and died, most by their own hand rather than face the crowd. Rebuilt in stone by Henry III, it served as a prison until 1929.
s: A quatrefoil keep and 1190's darkest night
_facts: Original motte-and-bailey castle built 1068 on William I's orders
In 1190, 150 local Jews died in the timber castle keep, most by suicide to avoid a mob
Henry III rebuilt it in stone with a unique quatrefoil-design keep in the mid-13th century
Used as a jail and prison until 1929; an explosion in 1684 wrecked its military use

w: Long before Vikings or Normans, this was Eboracum, provincial capital of Roman Britain and the largest town in the north. Two emperors died within its walls: Septimius Severus in 211 AD and Constantius Chlorus in 306 AD. The name may simply mean 'place of the yew trees' - York never really stopped being a capital.
_facts: Eboracum was the largest town in northern Britannia and a provincial capital
Septimius Severus died there in 211 AD and Constantius Chlorus in 306 AD
First recorded mention of the name is c. 95-104 AD on a Vindolanda tablet
The name may derive from a Brittonic root meaning 'yew tree place'

w: Come face to face with Mallard, the streamlined LNER engine still holding the world speed record for steam, parked alongside a Japanese bullet train and the Duchess of Hamilton under one roof. Part of the Science Museum Group, it won European Museum of the Year in 2001 - trainspotting's cathedral, and still expanding.
s: Home to Mallard, the fastest steam engine ever
_facts: Home to the national collection including Mallard, Duchess of Hamilton and a Japanese bullet train
Won European Museum of the Year Award in 2001
Part of the Science Museum Group
Station Hall, a Grade II listed former goods station of 1875-77, reopened in 2025 after repairs

w: Opened in 1830, the Yorkshire Museum has run the same five collections side by side ever since: biology, geology, archaeology, numismatics and astronomy, all under one antiquarian roof. A cabinet of curiosities that never got tidied into separate buildings.
_facts: Opened in 1830
Has five permanent collections: biology, geology, archaeology, numismatics and astronomy

w: Board a 'time capsule' carriage and ride slowly past life-size dioramas of Viking-age street life, lifelike mannequins going about their day to a soundtrack piped through hidden speakers. Built by York Archaeological Trust and opened in 1984, it borrowed its name - Jorvik - from the Viking kingdom that once ruled York.
s: Ride the time capsule into Viking York
_facts: Museum with lifelike mannequins and life-size dioramas of Viking life
Visitors ride through in 'time capsule' carriages with speakers
Created by York Archaeological Trust and opened in 1984
Name comes from Jorvik, the Old Norse name for York and the Viking Kingdom of Yorkshire

w: A social-history museum built inside a former prison is a fitting twist for York: the debtors' block and female jail, raised in the 1700s from stone quarried out of the castle's own ruins, now house recreated period streets. John L. Kirk founded it in 1938 - crime and punishment repurposed as Victorian nostalgia.
s: A prison turned museum of everyday life
_facts: Founded by John L. Kirk in 1938
Housed in the debtors' prison (built 1701-05 using stone from the castle ruins) and the female prison (built 1780-85)
Located on the site of York Castle, originally built by William the Conqueror in 1068

w: Three battles in three weeks decided 1066, and the first was fought here: Harald Hardrada's Vikings crushed the English at Fulford before marching on to their own defeat at Stamford Bridge - clearing the way for William's win at Hastings weeks later. Today it's known for its army barracks more than its bloodshed.
s: Where the Vikings won, weeks before Hastings
_facts: Site of the Battle of Fulford, won by the invading Vikings in 1066
A precursor to the Battle of Stamford Bridge (lost by the Vikings) and then the Battle of Hastings (won by the Normans) weeks later
Now home to Imphal Barracks, headquarters of the British Army's 15th Infantry Brigade and the Royal Military Police

w: A mile from the village, Wheldrake Ings floods each winter into a wet meadow of international importance, drawing rare wading birds and wildflowers few English fields still support. The land belonged to Fountains Abbey in the Middle Ages, then a private estate until the mid-20th century - now it belongs to the birds.
s: A wet meadow of international importance
_facts: Wheldrake Ings is a nature reserve of international importance a mile east of the village
Many wild flowers flourish and rare birds prosper there
The parish was largely in the possession of Fountains Abbey in the Middle Ages, then part of a landed estate until the mid-20th century
